seoDescription: Learn how to effectively separate your Django backend logic from your front-end presentation by using templates. This tutorial demonstrates how to create and manage HTML template files within your Django app structure. You'll see how to load templates in your views, pass data using a context dictionary, and dynamically render content with the Django Template Language (DTL). Discover the syntax for loops, conditional statements, and variables within your HTML, enabling you to build dynamic and maintainable web pages.

chapters.title: What Are Django Templates?
chapters.description: This chapter explains the concept of templates in Django and their role in separating front-end HTML from back-end logic.

chapters.title: Preparing the View to Load a Template
chapters.description: Learn how to prepare a Django view to use templates by cleaning up hardcoded HTML and importing the template loader.

chapters.title: Creating the Template Directory Structure
chapters.description: This section covers the conventional directory structure for storing template files within a Django application.

chapters.title: Writing a Basic HTML Template
chapters.description: Follow along to create a simple, generic HTML template with placeholder content for an album list.

chapters.title: Loading the Template and Creating Context
chapters.description: This chapter demonstrates how to load the template file in the view and create a context dictionary to pass data to it.

chapters.title: Rendering the Template with Context
chapters.description: Learn how to render the loaded template with the context data and return the final HTML as an HTTP response.

chapters.title: Using Django Template Language for Loops and Variables
chapters.description: This section introduces the Django Template Language (DTL) syntax for creating for-loops and inserting variables into HTML.

chapters.title: Checking the Result and Adding Conditional Logic
chapters.description: See the dynamic template in action and learn how to use if/else statements in DTL to handle cases where no data is available.

chapters.title: Conclusion and Next Steps
chapters.description: This final chapter recaps the core concepts of using Django templates and previews what's coming next.

summary:
## What are Django Templates? **Templates** are generic HTML files that separate your application's presentation layer from the Python backend logic. This allows web designers to create the structure and layout (the "blueprint") of a page with placeholder content, which developers can then dynamically populate with real data from the database. ## Setting Up and Using Templates The process involves creating the template file, loading it in the view, and passing data to it for rendering. ### 1. File Structure By convention, Django looks for templates inside a `templates` directory within each app. - Create a folder named `templates` in your app's root directory (e.g., `music/templates/`). - Inside that, create another folder with the same name as your app (e.g., `music/templates/music/`). - Place your HTML template files inside this nested directory (e.g., `music/templates/music/index.html`). > [!NOTE] > This namespacing (`app/templates/app/`) prevents template name collisions between different Django apps in the same project. ### 2. Loading the Template in a View In your `views.py`, use the `loader` to get a reference to your template file. ```python from django.template import loader from .models import Album def index(request): all_albums = Album.objects.all() # 1. Load the template template = loader.get_template('music/index.html') ``` ### 3. Passing Data with Context Data is passed from the view to the template using a **context dictionary**. The keys in the dictionary become variable names accessible within the template. ```python # 2. Create the context dictionary context = { 'all_albums': all_albums, } ``` ### 4. Rendering the Final HTML The final step is to `render` the template with the context and the request, then return it in an `HttpResponse`. ```python from django.http import HttpResponse # ... in the view function ... # 3. Render the template with context and return it return HttpResponse(template.render(context, request)) ``` ## Django Template Language (DTL) DTL provides syntax for embedding logic and variables directly into your HTML. ### **Variables** - Variables are enclosed in double curly braces: `{{ variable_name }}`. - You can access object attributes using dot notation: `{{ album.album_title }}`. ```html {{ album.album_title }} ``` ### **Tags** - Tags provide logic like loops and conditionals, enclosed in `{% ... %}`. - Common tags include `for`/`endfor` and `if`/`else`/`endif`. **For Loops:** To iterate over a list (like a QuerySet): ```html
    {% for album in all_albums %}
  • {{ album.album_title }}
    • {% endfor %}
``` > [!IMPORTANT] > Remember to close your block tags, for example, `{% for ... %}` requires a corresponding `{% endfor %}`. **Conditional Logic:** To check if data exists before displaying it: ```html {% if all_albums %}
    {% for album in all_albums %}
  • ...
    • {% endfor %}
{% else %}

You don't have any albums

{% endif %} ```
